tradition: The West Syriac (Syriac Orthodox) Church
presentBody: The Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch
namedGap: The Syriac Orthodox Church between 1300 and 1915
basis: The same church as the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says it continued under Muslim rule and now has congregations in the Middle East, India and the diaspora. The Sayfo and Syriac diaspora entry tells its twentieth century; no entry covers 1300 to 1915.

tradition: Chalcedonian monasticism of the Judean desert and Gaza
presentBody: The monasteries of Mar Saba and Saint Catherine at Sinai
namedGap: Judean desert and Sinai monasticism from 614 to today

evidence.title: Is the Burning Bush still burning? (supporters' site, text credited to the monastery's librarian)
evidence.quote: Priestmonk Arsenios, successor to long-time Monastery “Dikaios” Geronta Pavlos as the spiritual father in charge of the Monastery’s spiritual life

evidence.title: Ancient Palestinian monastery under UNESCO consideration (news report)
evidence.quote: Mar Saba Monastery is one of 13 Palestinian sites included on UNESCO's tentative lists

basis: Two houses of this tradition still have monks: Mar Saba in the Judean desert and Saint Catherine's at Sinai. The entry's own text says so. A 2017 page by Sinai's supporters names the monastery's present spiritual father, and a 2016 news report names Mar Saba as an existing monastery.
wanted: A dated statement from the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem or the Sinai monastery that names its present community.

tradition: The Benedictine monasticism of the Rule
presentBody: The Benedictine congregations and abbeys, including Monte Cassino
namedGap: Benedictine monasticism after 604; only the Cluniac and Cistercian reforms have entries

evidence.title: OSB.org home page, news item on the Pannonhalma chapter (timestamp 2026-10-09)
evidence.quote: The conventual chapter of Pannonhalma Archabbey has re-elected Archabbot Cirill Hortobágyi OSB for a further term as Archabbot.

basis: The Rule of Benedict is still lived in Benedictine abbeys. The order's own website carries news dated October 2026, including an abbot's re-election and a meeting of Benedictine educators at Melk Abbey. The entry's own text says monks live at Monte Cassino now.
wanted: An independent dated count of Benedictine houses, such as a Vatican yearbook or a scholarly survey.

tradition: The Roman Church under Gregory the Great
presentBody: The Catholic Church
namedGap: The Roman Church from 604 to about 1049
basis: An early period of the Roman Church, which the Catholic Church carries today. The entry's own text follows the Pastoral Rule and the papal government of central Italy into later centuries. The Latin papal church entry from about 1049 takes up the line.

tradition: The Latin church of Merovingian Gaul
presentBody: The Catholic Church
namedGap: The Latin church in the Frankish lands from 888 to about 1049
basis: A period of the Latin church in Gaul. The entry's own text says the same institution continued directly into Carolingian Christianity. The Catholic Church carries that Latin line today.

tradition: The church of Ireland in the age of Patrick and the monasteries
presentBody: The Catholic Church in Ireland and the Church of Ireland
namedGap: The Irish church from 1169 to today

evidence.title: Irish Catholic Bishops' Conference, home page with dated statements
evidence.quote: Nov 10, 2026 Archbishop Martin: Human trafficking is one of the great scandals of our world today

descentBasis: The Catholic Church in Ireland and the Church of Ireland both claim the early Irish church; the claim of the Church of Ireland was not checked, because its site refused the fetch.
basis: The church planted in Ireland is alive today in the Catholic Church in Ireland and the Church of Ireland. The Irish Catholic Bishops' Conference posts dated statements through November 2026. Both churches claim this early church, so the line of descent is open to dispute.
wanted: A dated Church of Ireland statement of its claim to the early Irish church, and an independent count of both churches such as the 2022 Irish census.

tradition: The church of Ireland from 664 to 1169
presentBody: The Catholic Church in Ireland and the Church of Ireland
namedGap: The Irish church from 1169 to today

evidence.title: Irish Catholic Bishops' Conference, home page with dated statements
evidence.quote: Nov 10, 2026 Archbishop Martin: Human trafficking is one of the great scandals of our world today

descentBasis: The Catholic Church in Ireland and the Church of Ireland both claim the early Irish church; the claim of the Church of Ireland was not checked, because its site refused the fetch.
basis: The church in Ireland between Whitby and the Anglo-Norman invasion is alive today in the Catholic Church in Ireland and the Church of Ireland. The Irish Catholic Bishops' Conference posts dated statements through November 2026. Both churches claim this church, so the line of descent is open to dispute.
wanted: A dated Church of Ireland statement of its claim to the early Irish church, and an independent count of both churches such as the 2022 Irish census.

tradition: Aksumite Christianity
presentBody: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church
basis: The same church as the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says it continued without interruption and still prays in Ge'ez. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Christianity entry holds the present-day evidence.

tradition: Georgian Christianity before 609
presentBody: The Georgian Orthodox Church
basis: The same church as the Georgian Orthodox Church, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says the body has carried on through the centuries to the present. The restored Georgian church entry holds the present-day evidence; no entry covers 1245 to 1917.

tradition: Christianity in the Nubian kingdoms before 652
basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says Christian Nubia faded in the later Middle Ages and no Nubian church continues today. What remains is buildings, murals and documents.

tradition: Homoian Christianity of the Goths and Vandals
basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says it ended in conversion, in Spain and among the Lombards by the seventh century. It left a Gothic Bible and buildings, but no community.
endQuote: Nothing continues this tradition today: it ended in conversion

tradition: The Church of Caucasian Albania
basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says no church carries on under this name, and its see was done away with early in the nineteenth century. Its people merged with the Armenians.
endQuote: No church carries on under this name.
openQuestion: The entry says the Udi people of Azerbaijan are generally seen as descended from its Christians; does a documented Udi church community today count as descent?

tradition: Latin Christianity in North Africa under Byzantium
basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says this church left no successor and Latin Christianity in North Africa had all but disappeared by the later Middle Ages. Its refusals to the emperor are remembered, but no community continued.

tradition: Nicene Christianity of Visigothic Iberia
presentBody: The Hispano-Mozarabic rite at Toledo Cathedral
basis: Its liturgy lives on. The entry's own text says the Mozarabic rite, formed in this period, is still celebrated in a chapel of Toledo Cathedral. The Mozarabic Christianity entry holds the dated evidence.
openQuestion: Does the Visigothic church count as alive through the Mozarabic rite alone, or through the whole Catholic Church in Spain?

tradition: The British church in Wales
presentBody: The Church in Wales
namedGap: The Welsh church from 1282 to today

evidence.title: Church in Wales home page (copyright line 2007-2026; news dated 6 October 2026)
evidence.publisher: The Representative Body of the Church in Wales
evidence.quote: Copyright © 2007-2026 The Representative Body of the Church in Wales. All Rights Reserved.

descentBasis: The entry's own text says the Welsh church carried on under its own bishops. The Church in Wales names the dioceses of St Asaph, Bangor, St Davids and Llandaff on its site, but no fetched source states that they continue the medieval sees.
basis: The Welsh church carried on under its own bishops after 768. The Church in Wales is alive today; its own site carries a 2026 copyright line and news dated October 2026. The entry itself says no separate British church continues.
wanted: A dated Church in Wales or scholarly statement that its sees continue the medieval Welsh church.
openQuestion: The entry says no separately continuing British church exists; does the Church in Wales count as the same tradition?

tradition: The Welsh church from 768 to 1282
presentBody: The Church in Wales
namedGap: The Welsh church from 1282 to today

evidence.title: Church in Wales home page (copyright line 2007-2026; news dated 6 October 2026)
evidence.publisher: The Representative Body of the Church in Wales
evidence.quote: Copyright © 2007-2026 The Representative Body of the Church in Wales. All Rights Reserved.

descentBasis: The entry's own text says the Welsh church carried on under its own bishops. The Church in Wales names the dioceses of St Asaph, Bangor, St Davids and Llandaff on its site, but no fetched source states that they continue the medieval sees.
basis: The Welsh church of this period is alive today as the Church in Wales. Its own site carries a 2026 copyright line and news dated October 2026. The link to the medieval sees still wants a source.
wanted: A dated Church in Wales or scholarly statement that its sees continue the medieval Welsh church.

tradition: Arabic-speaking Chalcedonian Christianity of Palestine and Syria
presentBody: The Melkite Greek Catholic Church and the Greek Orthodox churches of Antioch and Jerusalem
descentBasis: The entry's own text says the communion lives on in the Greek Orthodox churches of Antioch and Jerusalem and in the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. The tree links it to the Melkite Greek Catholic Church at the same level.
basis: The same communion lives on in the Melkite Greek Catholic Church and in the Greek Orthodox churches of Antioch and Jerusalem. The entry's own text says so. The Melkite Greek Catholic Church entry carries the line; no entry covers 1009 to 1724.

tradition: The English church from Augustine to Lindisfarne
presentBody: The Church of England and the Catholic Church in England
descentBasis: The entry's own text says the dioceses, cathedrals and parish network carried on into the later medieval English church. After the Reformation the Church of England and the Catholic Church in England both claim that line.
basis: The English church of this age continued. The entry's own text says its story runs straight on into the late Anglo-Saxon church. The Church of England and the Catholic Church in England both claim that line today.

tradition: The Carolingian reform of the Latin church
presentBody: The Catholic Church
namedGap: The Latin church from 888 to about 1049
basis: An episode of a living tradition. The Latin church it reformed is carried today by the Catholic Church. The entry's own text says its church law ran on into the papal reform of the eleventh century.

tradition: Byzantine monasticism in the age of the icon struggle
presentBody: The Orthodox monasteries of Mount Athos and the wider Orthodox monastic world
descentBasis: The entry's own text says Athonite monks are usually counted as the heirs of the Stoudite monks, though little survives to show the handover.
basis: Its monastic way of life carried on after 843. The entry's own text says Athonite monks are usually counted its heirs. The Athonite and Comnenian monasticism entry carries the line.

tradition: The Slavic Christianity of Cyril and Methodius
presentBody: The Bulgarian, Serbian and Russian Orthodox churches, and other Slavic churches
basis: Slavic worship in the Slavonic language carries on in the Slavic Orthodox churches. The entry's own text says Church Slavonic is still the language of worship in much of the Orthodox world. The Balkan and Russian church entries hold the present-day evidence.

tradition: The Christianity of Kievan Rus
presentBody: The Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian churches
descentBasis: The entry's own text names the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian Orthodox churches as heirs, so more than one body traces its founding to this church.
basis: The church founded by Vladimir continued into the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian churches. The entry's own text says so. More than one body claims the line, so the entry names the heirs but not a single one.

tradition: Mozarabic Christianity and its rite
presentBody: The Hispano-Mozarabic rite and its chapel at Toledo Cathedral
namedGap: The Mozarabic community from 1031 to today

evidence.title: Rito Hispano-Mozárabe (page metadata dateModified 2026-01-12)
evidence.quote: el rito vive en este espacio privilegiado, donde continúa celebrándose cada mañana

descentBasis: The entry's own text says only a small community at Toledo kept the name, and that Cardinal Cisneros rescued the rite around 1500. The cathedral's page says the rite has been celebrated each morning without a break since.
basis: The Mozarabic rite is alive at Toledo Cathedral. The cathedral's own page, with a 2026 modification date, says the rite is celebrated each morning. The entry's own text says only a small community kept the name into modern times.
wanted: An independent dated report that names the Mozarabic community or parishes of Toledo.

tradition: The Cluniac reform order

evidence.title: Cluny (Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 4; cited for the end date only)
evidence.quote: At the suppression in 1790 it was bought by the town and almost entirely destroyed.

basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says the order dwindled and its great church was quarried away after the French Revolution. The Catholic Encyclopedia dates the suppression to 1790. Its feast of All Souls is still kept, but that is influence, not a continuing order.

tradition: The St Thomas Christians of India
presentBody: The Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite churches, the Mar Thoma Church, and other St Thomas Christian churches of Kerala
namedGap: The St Thomas Christians from 1665 to 1836
basis: The community never stopped existing. The entry's own text says its descendants are the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, divided today among several churches. The Malankara and Mar Thoma entries carry the line.

tradition: The Paulicians
basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says nothing institutional survived the fall of Tephrike in 878. Later links to the Bogomils and Cathars rest on hostile sources and cannot be shown.
endQuote: Nothing institutional survived: the Paulician state ended with Tephrike in 878

tradition: The Bogomils of the tenth and eleventh centuries
basis: Its carriers ended. The later Balkan Bogomil entry says nothing continued, and no buildings, books or descendants remain. The Bogomils left no text of their own.
endQuote: Nothing continued, and almost nothing remains — no buildings, no books, no descendants.

tradition: The conversion of Scandinavia and the churches it founded
presentBody: The Church of Norway, the Church of Sweden, the Church of Denmark and the Church of Iceland

evidence.title: kirken.no home page, news item of 10.11.2026
evidence.quote: Den norske kirke har ressurser samfunnet trenger når kriser rammer

descentBasis: The entry's own text says the conversions founded the national churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland. The later Reformation entry says they became the Lutheran churches that are still the largest in their countries.
basis: The conversions founded the national churches of the Nordic kingdoms, which exist today. The Church of Norway's own site carries news dated 10 November 2026. These are Lutheran churches since the Reformation, which the entry's own text treats as a break in Denmark.
wanted: An independent dated count of membership in the Nordic national churches.
openQuestion: The Scandinavian Reformation Kingdoms entry says these churches still exist yet is flagged not living; should that entry be reviewed?

tradition: The Syriac Orthodox Church under the caliphs
presentBody: The Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch
namedGap: The Syriac Orthodox Church between 1300 and 1915
basis: The same church as the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says it exists with its own patriarch and a large worldwide diaspora. The Sayfo and Syriac diaspora entry holds the present-day evidence.

tradition: Makurian Nubian Christianity
basis: Its carriers ended. The entry's own text says Christian Nubia lasted into the fifteenth century in places, and no Nubian Christian community survives today. What remains is the Faras paintings.
endQuote: no Nubian Christian community survives today

tradition: The English church from Lindisfarne to the Conquest
presentBody: The Church of England and the Catholic Church in England
descentBasis: The entry's own text says the dioceses, cathedrals and parish network carried on into the later medieval English church. After the Reformation the Church of England and the Catholic Church in England both claim that line.
basis: The English church of this age continued. The entry's own text says its dioceses, cathedral communities and parish network carried on after the Conquest, and many cathedrals still stand where its bishops put them. The Church of England and the Catholic Church in England both claim that line today.

tradition: The Georgian monastic revival of Tao-Klarjeti and Athos
presentBody: The Georgian Orthodox Church
basis: The same tradition runs on into the Georgian Orthodox Church of today. The entry's own text says so, and Iviron is still one of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos. The restored Georgian church entry holds the present-day evidence.

tradition: Ethiopian Christianity from the fall of Aksum to the Zagwe
presentBody: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church
basis: The same church as the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which carries the tradition today. The entry's own text says the institution continued through these centuries. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Christianity entry holds the present-day evidence.
